title: As a designer, I get professional vector tools — pen and path editing, boolean operations, precise alignment — for real interface design work
As a designer, frames can behave responsively — auto layout, constraints, and grids resize designs the way real UIs flex
As a designer, I can build reusable components with variants and per-instance overrides that stay linked to their source
As a designer, I can manage design tokens or variables — colors, spacing, typography — with modes or themes applied across designs
As a designer, shared libraries publish components and styles across files and projects, with controlled updates when the source changes
As a designer, I can wire screens into clickable prototypes with triggers, transitions, and overlays — no code required
As a designer, prototypes can carry advanced behavior — animation between states, conditions or variables, scroll effects — to feel like the real product
As a developer, I can inspect any layer and get measurements, styles, assets, and code snippets (CSS/iOS/Android) without an editor seat
As a developer, designs map to production code — component-to-code mappings or direct design-to-code output I can actually ship
As a designer, my whole team can edit the same file simultaneously with live cursors and instant sync
As a product manager, I can comment directly on designs, mention teammates, and resolve threads so review happens in the file, not in email
As a designer, I can extend the editor from a large plugin community or marketplace — icons, data fillers, accessibility checkers, and more
As a developer, a documented plugin API with typings and samples lets me build and distribute my own editor extensions
As a designer, full version history lets me name milestones, compare, and restore any earlier state of a file
As a designer, I can export production assets — PNG, SVG, PDF, and more — with per-layer presets, scales, and slices
As a developer, the file format is open or documented, so my designs stay portable and toolable outside the vendor's editor
As a developer, I can self-host the full design platform on my own infrastructure under an open-source license
As a designer, I can generate or edit designs from a natural-language prompt — first drafts, layouts, or full mockups the tool actually produces
As a designer, built-in AI handles asset chores — image generation, background removal, content-aware fills, copy suggestions — inside the editor
As a designer, the free tier supports real design work — usable editor and collaboration without a paid seat
As a product manager, published plan pricing makes seat types, tiers, and AI-feature gating clear before procurement
As an AI-native user, my coding agent can pull real design context — frames, variables, screenshots, component mappings — through an MCP server or API to implement the design
As an AI-native user, an agent can create or modify designs programmatically — through a write-capable API, plugin surface, or MCP tools — not just read them
As an AI-native user, an agent can render and export designs — screenshots, images, or production formats — through a documented programmatic surface
